evidence: src/app/(app)/import/share/route.ts:46 isCrossSite: an Origin header that is present but does not parse as a URL is treated as cross-site (the catch at src/app/(app)/import/share/route.ts:54 returns true), and src/app/(app)/import/share/route.ts:59 answers it 403. The serialized opaque origin is the literal string null, and node -e 'new URL("null")' throws ERR_INVALID_URL (captured in this review), so a share POST carrying Origin: null is refused 403 before the file is read.

src/app/(app)/import/share/route.ts:29 asserts as present-tense fact that the share sheet POSTs from the installed app, whose origin is this site. Nothing in the artifact witnesses what Origin header the Android share sheet's POST actually carries: the share sheet's request is a browser-initiated navigation with no initiating document, which is exactly the case where a browser is entitled to send an opaque origin.

No test reaches that case: test/app/share-route.test.ts:100 covers a foreign origin, test/app/share-route.test.ts:107 this site's own origin, and every e2e share in test/e2e/share-target.spec.ts:86, test/e2e/share-target.spec.ts:123 and test/e2e/share-target.spec.ts:144 is sent by Playwright's API client with no Origin header at all, the one shape the route never refuses.
delivery/work-history/m3-p5.yaml:96 concedes installation and use on the owner's device were not witnessed, so the only caller the route exists for has never been observed against this check.
findings.concrete-fix: In src/app/(app)/import/share/route.ts, decide the cross-site question from what the real caller sends rather than from an assumed Origin: treat an Origin of exactly null (and an absent Origin) as not cross-site when Sec-Fetch-Site is none or same-origin, refuse when Sec-Fetch-Site is cross-site or same-site, and keep the host comparison for a parseable Origin. Add unit cases in test/app/share-route.test.ts for Origin: null with Sec-Fetch-Site none (accepted) and with Sec-Fetch-Site cross-site (refused). Correct the comment at route.ts:29 so it states what is known, and record in the work history that the request headers of a real Android share were not captured, as owed on-device evidence.
findings.analysis: This is the phase intent's one caller. If the share sheet's POST carries Origin: null, every real share on the owner's phone is a 403 and the phase delivers nothing on the device it was built for, while all 137 e2e tests stay green, because the suite never sends that header. I could not construct the device request in this container, so I rank it medium rather than high; confirmed, it would be high. The check is also stricter than its own stated purpose: the comment says a foreign page's form is the threat, and a parse failure is not evidence of a foreign page.
